summary: This standards-track document describes how to carry H.264 Scalable Video Coding (SVC) video in RTP packets. One video stream is encoded in layers, so receivers with weaker links or smaller screens can use just the layers they can handle. It explains how to pack and split the coded units across packets and how layers can be sent in one or several RTP sessions.

plainLanguage.summary: A video is built like a layer cake. Weak phones take only the bottom layers, strong TVs take the whole cake. This document explains how to put the layers into delivery boxes for the internet.

subtitle: How to carry layered H.264 SVC video in RTP so each receiver can take only the layers it can handle.

tldr.problem: Receivers differ in screen size, processing speed and network conditions, and conditions change over time. Sending one fixed-quality video stream, or many separate copies, adapts poorly to that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how to put the NAL units of H.264 Scalable Video Coding (SVC) into RTP packets, with new packet types such as PACSI that summarize layer information. It lets the layers travel in one RTP session or be split across several, with rules to recover the decoding order.
tldr.outcome: Network elements can drop layers without decoding the video, and the base layer stays readable by RFC 6184 receivers. It is a Standards Track document and the unit metadata lists no RFC that replaces it.

today: RFC 6190 is a Standards Track document (Proposed Standard), and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the H.264 payload format in RFC 6184.

sections.title: Scalable Video in RTP
sections.content:
RFC 6190 specifies an RTP payload format for the Scalable Video Coding (SVC) extension of H.264/AVC, defined in Annex G of ITU-T H.264. An SVC bitstream offers the source video at several levels of fidelity along three dimensions: spatial (picture size), quality (signal-to-noise ratio) and temporal (pictures per second). These are identified by the parameters dependency_id, quality_id and temporal_id.

Components are built in a pyramid: decoding one component needs all the components it depends on. An operation point is the set of components needed to decode one combination of those three values. The lowest layer, with dependency_id and quality_id both zero, is compliant with H.264/AVC by design.

Adaptation can happen at the source, at the destination or in an intermediate media-aware network element (MANE). Because an SVC stream contains an H.264/AVC compliant sub-stream, a MANE can easily filter out all SVC-specific information.
sections.plainLanguage: The video is stacked in layers, with a simple picture at the bottom and finer detail piled on top. Anyone can stop climbing at the layer that suits their device.

sections.title: The SVC NAL Unit Header
sections.content:
All coded data is wrapped in NAL units. H.264 has a one-byte NAL unit header with the fields F, NRI and Type. SVC uses three NAL unit types that H.264/AVC left reserved: type 14 for the prefix NAL unit, type 15 for the subset sequence parameter set and type 20 for the coded slice in scalable extension. Types 14 and 20 add three more octets to the header.

Those extra octets carry the layer identification: PRID (priority, where a lower value means higher priority), DID (dependency_id), QID (quality_id) and TID (temporal_id), plus flags such as I (IDR), N, U, D (discardable) and O (output). Section 4.2 explains how a MANE may use them, for example to protect NAL units with a lower DID, QID or TID better than those with higher values.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of video gets a small sticker saying which layer it belongs to and how important it is, so helpers along the way know what they may throw away.

sections.title: Transmission Modes and Packetization Modes
sections.content:
There are two basic transmission modes. In single-session transmission (SST) all layers travel in one RTP session. In multi-session transmission (MST) the layers are spread over two or more RTP sessions. SST SHOULD be used for point-to-point unicast, and MST SHOULD be used for multicast where different receivers need different operation points. If the mst-mode media type parameter is absent, SST MUST be used.

In SST the three packetization modes of RFC 6184 (single NAL unit, non-interleaved and interleaved) all apply. MST adds four modes that differ in whether interleaving is allowed and in how decoding order is recovered across sessions.

The base layer, when sent alone in its own RTP stream, must use the H.264 packetization of RFC 6184, so legacy receivers can join and read just that session. All receivers MUST support the non-interleaved mode, and the single NAL unit mode SHOULD be avoided whenever possible because small NAL units each wasting a packet header is inefficient.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send the whole cake in one box or put each layer in its own box. Separate boxes are handy when many people are watching and each wants a different amount of cake.

sections.title: Payload Structures and New NAL Unit Types
sections.content:
The RFC keeps the three basic payload structures of RFC 6184: the single NAL unit packet, the aggregation packet and the fragmentation unit. It adds three new NAL unit kinds. The PACSI NAL unit is type 30. The empty NAL unit and the NI-MTAP both use type 31, which is extended by one more octet holding a 5-bit Subtype (1 for empty, 2 for NI-MTAP) and three flag bits J, K and L. All other subtype values are reserved, and receivers MUST ignore the whole NAL unit for those.

An NI-MTAP is a non-interleaved multi-time aggregation packet. Each unit in it has a 16-bit NAL unit size and a 16-bit timestamp offset, so NAL units from different time instances can be grouped in decoding order. The earliest unit has an offset of zero. The empty NAL unit is only a two-byte header, used to keep timestamps aligned across sessions.

The payload header length depends on the type: four bytes when the type is 14, 20 or 30, two bytes when it is 31, and one byte otherwise. Fragmenting a NAL unit with the four-byte SVC header treats the three extension bytes as payload, so they appear only in the first fragment.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides the usual boxes, there are three new kinds: a label box that tells what is inside another box, an empty marker box, and a big box that holds pieces from several moments in time.

sections.title: The PACSI NAL Unit
sections.content:
The payload content scalability information (PACSI) NAL unit gives an informative summary of the layers in a packet, so a MANE does not have to look inside the video data. It also carries cross-session decoding order numbers and can improve loss resilience by repeating SEI messages and marking where a layer representation starts and ends. It MAY be carried in a single NAL unit packet or an aggregation packet and MUST NOT be fragmented. In an aggregation packet it MUST be the first aggregated unit.

Its first four octets are the standard SVC NAL unit header. One flags octet follows, with the bits X, Y, T, A, P, C, S and E. Optional fields TL0PICIDX, IDRPICID and DONC appear only when the Y or T bit is set. The header fields summarize the remaining NAL units, for example the PRID, DID, QID and TID take the lowest value found.

Several flags are shortcuts. A marks an anchor layer representation, a possible random access point; P says the content is only redundant slices that can be discarded; C says intra slices are present; S and E mark the first and last VCL NAL unit of a layer representation.
sections.plainLanguage: The PACSI is a label on the outside of a package saying what layers are inside. A helper can read it and decide to pass the package on or drop it without opening it.

sections.title: Recovering Decoding Order Across Sessions
sections.content:
When layers arrive in several sessions, the receiver has to merge the NAL units back into the correct decoding order. The four MST modes do this in different ways and are signaled by mst-mode.

In NI-T, timestamps align the sessions. Every access unit present in one session must also have some NAL unit in each enhancement session that depends on it, and empty NAL units are the way to fill gaps. The receiver collects NAL units with the same media timestamp, orders them by session dependency and then orders them within the access unit with an informative algorithm (Table 12).

In NI-C and I-C, a cross-session decoding order number (CS-DON) says the order explicitly. It is coded in the DONC field of PACSI NAL units or derived from them, and wraps modulo 65536. The receiver holds NAL units in a re-multiplexing buffer and releases them in increasing CS-DON distance. NI-TC offers both methods and the receiver picks one.
sections.plainLanguage: If a book is torn into chapters and sent by several couriers, page numbers or time stamps let you put the pages back in order. This document offers both.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Signaling
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type video/H264-SVC. It has no required parameters but many optional ones. Examples are profile-level-id, which gives the default sub-profile and level, and mst-mode, which selects MST and its packetization mode. Receivers MUST ignore any parameter they do not know, which keeps future extensions backward compatible. The RFC also includes parameters for the re-multiplexing buffer, and sprop-avc-ready says whether the stream can be converted to an RFC 6184 stream by dropping packets.

For MST, session dependencies are signaled with the rules of RFC 5583 and the order given by a=depend runs from the base session (most important) to the highest enhancement session (least important). The RFC gives SDP offer/answer examples, and parameter sets for a session SHOULD be sent in that session, MAY be sent in a session it depends on, and MUST NOT be sent in one it does not depend on.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the video starts, both sides trade a short note saying which layers they can handle and how they will be packed.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6184 apply. In addition, decoders MUST be careful with reserved NAL unit types and reserved SEI messages, and the safest way is to discard them. Integrity protection must account for the fact that a receiver may see only part of a scalable stream.

End-to-end authentication, integrity or confidentiality prevents a MANE from doing media-aware work beyond discarding whole packets, and confidentiality prevents even that. To work, a MANE has to be a trusted entity included in the security context, for both the media path and RTCP.

For congestion control, RFC 6184 applies, and a sender can cut the bit rate by removing NAL units with a high QID, TID, DID or PRID, or by application-specific rules. Removing packets means RTCP must be rewritten as RFC 3550 describes.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers on the road can only pick which boxes to drop if they are allowed to peek at the labels. If the labels are locked, they have to treat every box the same.
